title: jnana: Shankara's *Vivekachudamani* (selections)
hook: a student begs to be saved, and the teacher answers: fear not, and then, nobody can eat your dinner for you
carry: there's no one to free you but yourself

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Vivekachudamani calls seeking your own nature bhakti. To love the truth of who you are.

The student arrives at the teacher's feet in a state. In the Vivekachudamani he describes himself as scorched, caught in the forest fire of the world, shaken by the winds of misfortune. He has no list of questions. He has one request: save me. It's a request people carry into doctors' offices and counselors' rooms too. What a teacher says first, in that moment, shapes everything after. The book records it. And a little later, it records something harder.
screen: `THE STUDENT ARRIVES SCORCHED.` → `ONE REQUEST: SAVE ME.` → `WHAT DOES THE TEACHER SAY?`

segments.voice: The guru's first words, in paraphrase: fear not, wise one. There is no danger for you. There is a way across this ocean, the way the sages crossed, and I will show it to you. That's comfort, plainly given. No lecture on why the student is suffering. Just: you're not lost; there's a road. Then the student finds his questions. What is bondage? How did it come? How does it stay? How do I get free? The teacher praises him for asking. Then comes the harder part. A father in debt, the text says, has sons and others to pay it off. But for bondage, there's no one to free you but yourself. Someone else can lift a heavy load from your head. Hunger, though, goes away only when you eat. A sick person gets well by taking the medicine and keeping to the diet, not by someone else doing it for them. Later the text sharpens it: an illness isn't cured by saying the word medicine without drinking it. Fear not, and nobody can do this for you. They sound opposite, but the book holds them together. In the book, the teacher really can show the way, and does. What he can't do is walk it in the student's place. On this path, jnana isn't handed over like a parcel. It has to be eaten, so to speak, by the one who is hungry. That isn't harsh. It's the respect you give a grown friend: I'll sit with you, and I trust you to stand up.
screen: `FEAR NOT. THERE IS A WAY ACROSS.` · `A DEBT CAN BE PAID BY OTHERS.` · `HUNGER ENDS ONLY WHEN YOU EAT.` · `SAYING MEDICINE DOESN'T CURE.` · then, large: `I'LL SHOW YOU. YOU WALK.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one thing you've been hoping someone else would fix for you, a worry, a habit, a decision, and hold it lightly while the teacher's words land: fear not, there is a way across. After a few breaths, ask without any scolding what one small step on it is yours alone to take, and just see it clearly. If you pray, you can hold both the comfort and the step together.
Jnana. Knowing that frees. In the Vivekachudamani a teacher can show it, but like food or medicine, it works only for the one who takes it.
Your line: there's no one to free you but yourself. The teacher shows the road; the student walks it. Day nine hundred ninety-five, done.

howItsDone: In Advaita Vedanta the teacher, the guru, is held to be essential for showing the way, while the student is expected to reflect and meditate on the teaching personally until it becomes their own.

original.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: guru, teacher. In the Vivekachudamani the guru shows the way across, and the student walks it.

trapdoor: what you thought: a guru does the work of freeing you.
what it means: the teacher comforts and shows the way, but like eating or medicine, the student has to take it.
what a scholar hears: Vivekachudamani's debt, load and hunger images, and the medicine that cures only when drunk, not named.

chat.says: Can't a good teacher just hand you freedom, so you don't have to work at it?
options: In this book the teacher shows the way, but like eating, you have to do it.
Yes. In this book the teacher frees the student the moment he asks for help.
No. In this book the teacher refuses to help and sends the student away.
